questions.question: What is the core production invariant for machine translation?
options: Release only when meaning and protected facts remain attributable to the source.
Always choose the candidate with the highest model probability.
Use one global quality score for every language.
Translate every request even when the language pair is unsupported.
questions.explanation: Fluency and model preference do not excuse changed numbers, missing placeholders, unsafe additions, or unsupported source meaning.

questions.question: Why should tokenizer and model versions be deployed as one compatibility bundle?
options: A mismatched tokenizer can change token IDs, language tags, segmentation, and decoded output even when model weights are unchanged.
The tokenizer controls only UI font selection.
Model weights automatically infer every tokenizer version.
Tokenizer changes affect training but never serving.
questions.explanation: The model learned against a specific representation contract. Serving with a different tokenizer or normalization policy can corrupt inputs and outputs.

questions.question: A peak workload is 1,500 requests/s with 95 target tokens/request. What target-token rate must the fleet sustain before headroom?
options: 15,750 target tokens/s
95,000 target tokens/s
142,500 target tokens/s
1,425,000 target tokens/s
questions.explanation: Multiply request rate by generated target tokens: 1,500 x 95 = 142,500 target tokens per second.

questions.question: Why can a wider beam produce a candidate that must still be rejected?
options: Beam search optimizes model score, which does not guarantee terminology, placeholder, number, or source-faithfulness constraints.
Every beam wider than one removes punctuation.
Wider beams cannot discover additional hypotheses.
Beam search translates only high-resource languages.
questions.explanation: Search and release are separate decisions. Deterministic and quality gates still apply to the selected candidate.

questions.question: An aggregate semantic score is 90, but the Arabic emergency slice has two critical errors. What should a zero-critical-error policy do?
options: Ship because the aggregate score is high.
Block the release until that required slice passes.
Remove the Arabic slice from the report.
Average the error count with a larger language.
questions.explanation: A governed release is the conjunction of required slice gates. Aggregate performance cannot compensate for critical local failures.

questions.question: Which evaluation portfolio gives the strongest release evidence?
options: BLEU alone on one mixed-language test set
Latency alone because fast output is easier to review
Reference metrics, source-aware semantic metrics, deterministic invariants, slice analysis, and targeted human error review
Model log probability with no reference or source checks
questions.explanation: The methods catch different failures. Their combination is stronger than treating any one metric as complete.

questions.question: What is the safest degraded behavior when a high-impact translation cannot meet its evidence contract?
options: Return the most fluent candidate without a warning.
Bypass the glossary to reduce latency.
Hold or abstain and route to the approved fallback or human review path.
Retry indefinitely after the caller deadline.
questions.explanation: High-impact content should fail into an explicit accountable path rather than silently lowering the release standard.
